---
title: "Set-based enrichment — genes and species"
subtitle: "Notebook 05 results, with every check that earned them"
format: typst
---

# 1. The ranking

Raw counts from week 18 (157 participants), genes with ≥ 10 reads in a quarter
of samples. DESeq2 on `~ outcome`, contrast preterm vs term, ranked by the
Wald statistic.

```{r}
#| label: ranking
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(tidyverse); library(here)})
genes <- read_csv(here("data", "genes_by_outcome.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
cat("genes tested:", sum(!is.na(genes$pvalue)),
    "| significant (padj < 0.05):", sum(genes$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    "| positive stat (preterm-high):", sum(genes$stat > 0, na.rm = TRUE))
```

The column order of the count matrix was checked against the metadata rows
before the test (`stopifnot(identical(...))` — it passed).

# 2. fgsea against Hallmark

Ranking vector: `stat`, named by Ensembl ID. Hallmark sets from msigdbr with
Ensembl IDs. `fgsea(minSize = 15, maxSize = 500)`.

```{r}
#| label: hallmark
fg <- read_csv(here("data", "fgsea_hallmark_outcome.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
cat("sets tested:", nrow(fg), "| significant:", sum(fg$padj < 0.05),
    "| higher in preterm:", sum(fg$padj < 0.05 & fg$NES > 0),
    "| higher in term:", sum(fg$padj < 0.05 & fg$NES < 0))
fg |> arrange(padj) |> select(pathway, size, NES, padj) |> head(10) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 3)))
```

# 3. Two views of the fgsea result

```{r}
#| label: nesbar
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
fg |>
  slice_max(abs(NES), n = 12) |>
  mutate(pathway = str_to_sentence(str_replace_all(str_remove(pathway, "HALLMARK_"), "_", " ")),
         direction = if_else(NES > 0, "higher in preterm", "higher in term")) |>
  ggplot(aes(NES, reorder(pathway, abs(NES)), fill = direction)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Normalised enrichment score (NES)", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "Twelve strongest Hallmark sets") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: runscore
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(msigdbr)})
stat_vec <- genes$stat; names(stat_vec) <- genes$feature
stat_vec <- sort(stat_vec[!is.na(stat_vec)], decreasing = TRUE)
hh <- if (packageVersion("msigdbr") >= "10.0.0") {
  msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H")
} else {
  msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", category = "H")
}
tnfa <- hh |> distinct(gs_name, ensembl_gene) |>
  filter(gs_name == "HALLMARK_TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB") |> pull(ensembl_gene)
fgsea::plotEnrichment(tnfa, stat_vec) +
  labs(title = "Running score: HALLMARK_TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The running score climbs steeply at the left (the most preterm-positive
statistics) and reaches its maximum deviation with 115 of 195 genes in the
leading edge — the plot you would show if the identifiers had NOT matched
would hug zero instead.

# 4. Did the identifiers match?

- All 13,738 ranking names are clean `ENSG00000000000` format — no symbols, no
  version suffixes.
- **3,854 of 13,738** genes appear in at least one Hallmark set (Hallmark has
  only 4,391 genes total, so that is a high match rate, not a low one).
- The match is real, not luck: gene symbols against Ensembl IDs would have
  overlapped **zero** times; versioned IDs (`ENSG00000000000.1`) would also
  have overlapped zero times.

# 5. The top five sets, interpreted

1. **TNFα signalling via NF-κB** (NES 3.47, preterm-high): leading edge is a
   textbook NF-κB program — IL6, NFKB1, NFKBIA, TNFAIP3, ICAM1, CCL2.
2. **Inflammatory response** (NES 3.36, preterm-high): the broad cytokine/
   chemokine program — largely the same genes as #1.
3. **Heme metabolism** (NES −2.84, term-high): shares almost no genes with the
   others — a genuinely independent result; read cautiously (bulk tissue can
   track cell-type mix).
4. **Interferon gamma response** (NES 2.41, preterm-high): overlaps #2 partly,
   not a duplicate.
5. **Complement** (NES 2.38, preterm-high): independently plausible —
   complement is known to be involved in parturition.

## Shared genes between the top five sets

```{r}
#| label: shared
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(msigdbr)})
h <- if (packageVersion("msigdbr") >= "10.0.0") {
  msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H")
} else {
  msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", category = "H")
}
sets <- h |> distinct(gs_name, ensembl_gene) |> with(split(ensembl_gene, gs_name))
top5 <- fg |> arrange(padj) |> slice_head(n = 5) |> pull(pathway)
pr <- utils::combn(top5, 2)
map_dfr(1:ncol(pr), function(i) {
  a <- pr[1, i]; b <- pr[2, i]
  s <- length(intersect(sets[[a]], sets[[b]]))
  tibble(pair = paste(str_remove(a, "HALLMARK_"), "~", str_remove(b, "HALLMARK_")),
         shared = s, pct = round(100 * s / length(sets[[a]])))
}) |> arrange(desc(shared))
```

The top two sets share 51 genes and 32 leading-edge genes (IL6, NFKB1,
NFKBIA, TNFAIP3, CCL2, ICAM1…): the honest summary is **one finding** — an
NF-κB/cytokine program higher in preterm — not two. Heme metabolism overlaps
the rest at 0–5 genes.

# 6. Is the ranking balanced enough to trust fgsea?

```{r}
#| label: balance
stat_vec <- genes$stat; names(stat_vec) <- genes$feature
stat_vec <- sort(stat_vec[!is.na(stat_vec)], decreasing = TRUE)
ranked <- abs(stat_vec)
sig <- stat_vec[names(stat_vec) %in% genes$feature[which(genes$padj < 0.05)]]
top500 <- stat_vec[ranked >= quantile(ranked, 1 - 500 / length(ranked))]
tibble(slice   = c("all genes", "padj < 0.05", "top 500 by |stat|"),
       n       = c(length(stat_vec), length(sig), length(top500)),
       pct_pos = c(round(100 * mean(stat_vec > 0), 1),
                   round(100 * mean(sig > 0), 1),
                   round(100 * mean(top500 > 0), 1)))
```

At the 500 strongest genes the ranking is a coin flip (≈ 50% positive). The
sets that came out significant did so because their member genes **cluster**,
not because the whole transcriptome leaned one way.

# 7. Alternatives side by side

**Hypergeometric on significant genes only** (universe = 13,738 tested genes,
padj < 0.05 cutoff, BH correction): 19 sets significant among up genes — TNFα
signalling, inflammatory response, IL6/JAK/STAT3, complement, IL2/STAT5 — and
1 among down genes: heme metabolism.

**Comparison on the same 50 Hallmark sets** (fgsea vs hypergeometric):

```{r}
#| label: compare
cmp <- read_csv(here("data", "hallmark_methods_side_by_side.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
count(cmp, direction_agrees) |> arrange(desc(n))
```

Every strong result is found by both methods, directions never disagree. The
hypergeometric threw away information: a gene at padj = 0.049 counts the same
as one at 1e-40, and genes significant in the other direction count against
their set. fgsea uses the whole ranking.

**fgsea on Reactome** (1,056 sets): 359 significant (210 preterm-high). Top:
neutrophil degranulation (preterm); translation elongation/initiation and
ribosome quality control (term) — the same inflammation and growth programs,
at finer granularity.

# 8. The species table: 53 features

Default size factors gave 53 tested / **19 significant** species; with
**poscounts** size factors, **0** remain. All 19 were artifacts of library
composition — the poscounts table is the one used below.

```{r}
#| label: species
species <- read_csv(here("data", "species_by_outcome.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
species_stat <- species$stat; names(species_stat) <- species$feature
species_stat <- sort(species_stat[!is.na(species_stat)], decreasing = TRUE)
gc <- table(species$Genus)
genus_sets <- species |>
  filter(Genus %in% names(gc[gc >= 2])) |>
  with(split(feature, Genus))
fgg <- fgsea::fgsea(stats = species_stat, pathways = genus_sets,
                    minSize = 2, maxSize = 50) |> as.data.frame() |>
  arrange(padj) |> as_tibble()
cat("genus sets:", length(genus_sets),
    "| sizes:", paste(sort(lengths(genus_sets), decreasing = TRUE), collapse = ", "),
    "| any padj < 0.05:", any(fgg$padj < 0.05))
fgg |> select(pathway, size, NES, pval, padj) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 3)))
```

The top genus is Actinomyces (2 species, NES −1.41) and the top family is its
own Actinomycetaceae — the two levels agree on the same non-finding. Nothing
is significant: sets of 2–12 species give fgsea almost no power. The plain
sorted table (`data/species_sorted_by_stat.csv`, top: *Gardnerella
swidsinskii*, stat 2.02) reaches the same conclusion without enrichment.

# Choices made

- Ranked genes by the DESeq2 Wald `stat`; alternative: `log2FoldChange` (ignores uncertainty).
- Contrast preterm vs term, so NES > 0 means higher in preterm; alternative: the reverse (sign flips).
- Gene filter: ≥ 10 reads in a quarter of the week-18 samples; alternative: stricter/looser filters.
- Week 18 only (157 samples); alternative: all 471 samples across visits.
- Hallmark from msigdbr as **Ensembl IDs**; alternative: gene symbols (would have matched zero times).
- fgsea `minSize = 15, maxSize = 500`, seed 42; alternative: no size filter.
- Hypergeometric universe: the 13,738 tested genes; alternative: all 14,226 (would count untested genes as absent).
- Hypergeometric on padj < 0.05 up and down lists; alternative: fold-change cutoffs.
- Reactome (`C2`, `CP:REACTOME`) as the second collection; alternative: KEGG or GO.
- Species filter: present in ≥ 10% of week-18 samples; alternative: presence in all samples.
- **poscounts size factors** for the species test; alternative: default size factors (19 spurious hits).
- Genus sets with ≥ 2 species, fgsea `minSize = 2, maxSize = 50`; alternative: `minSize = 15` (excludes everything).
- No samples dropped; no genes or species beyond the filters above.
